passage: Anirban, you're frowning about your goal today. Sit, and I'll tell you about mine. I am Dolma, and at eleven I hit the last point that won our volleyball game in Leh. I jumped up screaming. Then I saw Tenzin, who had wanted that last spike all season, standing with his arms folded, silent. He didn't come to the tea afterwards. I knew why. I walked over and said, "Your pass set that up, you know. I couldn't have hit it without you." He shrugged, but his shoulders came down. I didn't pretend I hadn't scored, either. I said, "The next one is yours, if you're ready." He smiled a little.

qa.q: Where did Dolma win her volleyball game?
qa.a: In a volleyball game in Leh.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling after Dolma's winning point?
qa.a: Envy or disappointment, since he had wanted that last spike all season and stood silent with his arms folded.

qa.q: What could Anirban do if a teammate sulks after his goal?
qa.a: Credit the teammate's pass, include him, and still be honest that he scored. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when Dolma credited his pass?
qa.a: A little better: he shrugged, but his shoulders came down and he smiled a little.

grounding: An elder recalls scoring the winning point while a teammate who wanted that chance went quiet; she credited his pass and included him without hiding her own goal.

passage:
I was watching Santosh play ludo with Rohan on the verandah steps. Rohan went to get water. Santosh's counter was one square short of home, and his hand hovered over it. He glanced at the door. I don't know what he was thinking. Then he pulled his hand back, sat on it, and waited. When Rohan returned, Santosh rolled a two and lost by one turn. He said, "Good game." Later he muttered to me that a win like that would have felt fake, and he'd have had to hide it.

- Hansa

qa.q: What was Rohan doing when Santosh's hand hovered over the counter?
qa.a: Rohan had gone to get water.

qa.q: What might Santosh have been thinking and wanting when his hand hovered over the counter?
qa.a: Whether to bend the rule and win: he glanced at the door, then pulled his hand back, and later said a win like that would have felt fake and he'd have had to hide it.

qa.q: How could Santosh handle the urge next time?
qa.a: Keep his hands away from the board, roll fairly, and remember that a win by cheating feels empty.

qa.q: How would Rohan feel if he learned Santosh had left the counter alone?
qa.a: He would probably feel respected and safe playing with Santosh, since the game was fair.

grounding: A child is tempted to bend a rule when nobody would notice, but plays fair because a cheating win would feel empty and need hiding, seen by a friend.

passage:
Saturday. At the community centre final, Aditi quietly moved her counter two squares ahead while Ishita turned to sip water. She won, and everyone clapped. Ishita hugged her.

Sunday. The trophy sat on her shelf like a stone. She couldn't finish breakfast, and every time her mother said, "So proud," her stomach dropped.

Wednesday. Aditi went to Coach Meena's office, hands cold. "I cheated in the final," she said. "I moved my counter." The coach was quiet, then said the trophy would go to Ishita and Aditi would sit out the next tournament. Aditi cried, but on the walk home her chest felt lighter, like a fresh start.

qa.q: What did Aditi move during the final?
qa.a: Her counter, two squares ahead.

qa.q: What did the trophy feel like to Aditi on Sunday, and why?
qa.a: Heavy, like a stone, because guilt was working on her: she couldn't finish breakfast and her stomach dropped when her mother said "So proud."

qa.q: Why was going to the coach better than hiding it?
qa.a: Hiding it would let the guilt grow, while admitting it meant accepting a consequence and starting clean.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when she learns about the trophy?
qa.a: Possibly hurt by the cheating but glad to hear the truth, since she had hugged Aditi believing the win was fair.

grounding: A child cheats and wins, feels the trophy is heavy, admits it to the coach, accepts a consequence and starts clean.

passage: In the library games club in Toronto, Rania saw Jin slip a captured checker back onto the board while she reached for her juice. Heat rushed to her face. She wanted to shout "Cheater!" and sweep the board off the table. She even thought about sneaking a piece back herself. Instead she pressed her palms to her knees, counted five slow breaths, and walked to the volunteer at the desk. "Excuse me, I think a piece was moved back. Can you come and look?" Her voice shook a little. The volunteer came over, asked both players calmly what happened and reset the game. Rania felt the anger cool, though her heart still thumped.

qa.q: What did Rania see Jin do?
qa.a: She saw him slip a captured checker back onto the board while she reached for her juice.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling, and what did she consider doing before she asked for help?
qa.a: She was furious: she wanted to shout "Cheater!", sweep the board off the table, or sneak a piece back herself.

qa.q: Why was asking the volunteer wiser than cheating back?
qa.a: Cheating back would turn her into the same thing, while a calm report let an adult sort it out.

qa.q: How might Jin feel when the volunteer asks what happened?
qa.a: Probably nervous or embarrassed at being found out, and he may wonder what will happen next.

grounding: A child catches someone cheating against her, feels furious, and calmly tells the volunteer instead of accusing loudly or cheating back.

passage: The science-model deadline was tomorrow morning, and a power cut had plunged the flat into darkness. Nazia glued tiny paper leaves by torchlight, her fingers sticky. Bidisha had sent only silly stickers on the group chat all week, while the other two chatted about a cartoon. Nazia's jaw tightened. At first she wanted to keep doing everything in silence and glare at them. Instead she typed on her mother's phone: "I've done the model and both charts. Can you write the labels, and Rehan bring the poster? Please tell me by 8 tonight." Bidisha replied, "Sorry! I'll do labels now." Nazia decided that if it happened again, she would tell the teacher.

qa.q: What happened to the lights on the night before the deadline?
qa.a: There was a power cut, so Nazia worked by torchlight.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling toward her group, and how do you know?
qa.a: She was fuming and resentful: her jaw tightened after she had done the model and both charts while the others chatted.

qa.q: What could Nazia do if the others still do not help?
qa.a: Tell the teacher calmly what she has done and what is still undone.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Nazia's message?
qa.a: She replied "Sorry! I'll do labels now," so she likely saw it as a clear, fair request and realised she had been slack.

grounding: A child who did most of the project while others chatted feels resentful, clearly asks for tasks to be split, and plans to tell the teacher if it continues.

passage:
Our social studies group had four people making a chart about rivers. Sangeeta kept saying, "You're so good at this, you'll finish anyway," and drew doodles in her notebook. She did the same on Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday the teacher stopped by and looked at the pile of pages, all in Aarav's and Farida's handwriting. Sangeeta went red and looked at the floor. After the bell she said, "I've been slack. Give me the map and the title, and I'll do them tonight." Aarav shrugged. Next day the map was done, coloured carefully. I can't say why she changed; maybe it was the teacher's look.

- Gopika

qa.q: Which parts did Sangeeta ask for after the bell?
qa.a: The map and the title.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling when the teacher looked at the pages and she went red?
qa.a: Embarrassed or guilty, perhaps because the pages were all in other people's handwriting, though Gopika says she can't be sure why Sangeeta changed.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do to keep her share fair for the rest of the project?
qa.a: Take a real task from the start, check in with the group, and say so if she slips.

qa.q: How might Aarav and Farida have felt while Sangeeta doodled?
qa.a: Probably tired and unappreciated doing all the pages, though the passage only shows Aarav shrugging when she offered to help.

grounding: A child lets others do the work assuming they will finish anyway, then admits being slack and takes a real share, seen by a group mate.

passage: In the Class 6 art room in Kolkata, Nazia took the marker out of Bidisha's hand. "Not there. The title goes at the top, in blue." She rearranged every picture Ravi had pasted. Bidisha stepped back and folded her arms. Ravi went to sharpen a pencil that did not need sharpening. Nazia's poster looked neat, but the room had gone quiet. She noticed the dragging feet and the glance between the other two. "Do you have an idea?" she asked, slower. Bidisha said, "I wanted the river drawn in a curve." "Fine, you do the river. Ravi does the labels." It was not perfect; the curve wobbled. But everyone was talking again.

qa.q: What colour did Nazia say the title should be?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling when she stepped back and folded her arms?
qa.a: Shut out and maybe annoyed, since her marker was taken and she had an idea for the river that nobody had asked about.

qa.q: What could Nazia keep doing to make the project feel shared?
qa.a: Ask for ideas, give each person a part, and accept that the result may be a bit wobbly.

qa.q: How might Ravi see the situation?
qa.a: He went to sharpen a pencil that did not need sharpening, so he probably felt uncomfortable and unneeded while Nazia took over.

grounding: A child takes over the project because she thinks only her way is right, then notices others feel shut out, listens, and gives each person a part.

passage: I'm Manjula. In our group project on the solar system, Shreya gave me only tiny jobs, like cutting paper strips and fetching the glue. When I said I had an idea for a moving model, she said, "Maybe later," and turned away. I felt small, like a chair nobody notices. The next day I took a breath and said in a calm voice, "I drew my idea here. Can I make the moving part?" Shreya looked at the drawing and said, "Oh. Okay." If she had ignored me again, I planned to tell our teacher without being rude. I got the moving part, and I made the planet ring.

qa.q: What tiny jobs did Manjula get?
qa.a: Cutting paper strips and fetching the glue.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when Shreya said "Maybe later"?
qa.a: Small, like a chair nobody notices.

qa.q: What could Manjula do if Shreya keeps ignoring her ideas?
qa.a: Tell the teacher without being rude, as she planned.

qa.q: How might Shreya have seen Manjula's drawing?
qa.a: She said "Oh. Okay," which suggests she may not have realised how much Manjula had to offer until she saw it.

grounding: A child given only tiny jobs feels small, calmly shows her idea and asks for a bigger role, with the teacher as a fallback.

passage: I'm Ayesha. My part of our group poster on birds was a mess: crooked lines and two spelling mistakes. When the bell rang I ran to catch my bus, but Keerthana stayed behind for another hour and redid it without saying a word about it. The next morning I saw the poster and my ears felt hot. I felt thankful and a bit guilty. I said, "Thank you, Keerthana. I'm sorry you had to stay. Next time I'll check mine first." She smiled. This week I finished my share early and helped her with the border.

qa.q: What was wrong with Ayesha's part of the poster?
qa.a: It had crooked lines and two spelling mistakes.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she saw the fixed poster?
qa.a: Thankful and a little guilty, and her ears felt hot.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do to keep the group healthy?
qa.a: Say thank you clearly and do her own share carefully and on time, as she did this week.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt about staying behind?
qa.a: She did not complain and she smiled at Ayesha's thanks, so she may have been glad to help and glad to be noticed. 🙂

grounding: A group mate stays late to fix the child's part without complaint; the child feels grateful and guilty, says thank you and does her share next time.

passage:
Kalyani here, group mate. After school Arnab waited by the teacher's desk holding our folder. "Ma'am, could you look at who did what?" he asked. "I wrote the first page and the chart. Kalyani did the map. Two parts are still empty." He did not say anyone was bad. The teacher asked us to stay five minutes and check the folder together. I was worried Arnab would tell on me, and my face felt hot, but he also said my map was neat. Then the teacher split up the empty parts. Arnab never asked for extra marks for himself.

- Kalyani

qa.q: What did Arnab say he had written himself?
qa.a: The first page and the chart.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as Arnab spoke to the teacher?
qa.a: Worried and a bit hot in the face, expecting to be blamed, though Arnab also said her map was neat.

qa.q: Why is Arnab asking the teacher not tale-telling?
qa.a: He stuck to calm facts about who did what, without blaming anyone or asking for extra marks.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Arnab's request?
qa.a: As a fair request for help with an uneven group, since it was calm and factual.

grounding: A child asks the teacher to see who did what, describing facts calmly without blame and without claiming all the credit, seen by a group mate.
